P1.evidence: Read back the application including its limits — 'I saw your application. But there's not a lot in there' — and framed the call with an explicit disqualification promise: 'if there's a way and a potential that we can help you, that's cool. If not, I will guide you the best possible way I can.' Frame agreement was asked and given: 'Cool, man?' / 'Yep. Absolutely. Sounds good. Let's go for it.' The open question was clean: 'So, tell me. What's the biggest thing that you're working on right now?' Only the four-part structure is short — two parts, with nothing about what is in the way or what he needs.

P2.evidence: Seven of nine checks run, most of them properly. Work and desk-bound status were confirmed directly. The injury sequence was two-stage and effective — 'do you feel any stiffness in your lower back, hip?' then 'apart from the regular stiffness, did you have any injuries, something in the past that's appearing somewhere?' — which surfaced both the chronic trap and lower back pain and the historic soccer back injury. Diet was asked well and disarmed first: 'what are you eating right now? Like, and be honest, I'm not judging', producing a full inventory including the vegetarian constraint and his wife's egg allergy. Sleep was asked, and the rep did the valuable thing of noticing the contradiction and chasing it: 'But you mentioned that you wake up tired still.' The gaps: age was asked only as a late rhetorical check ('you're 35, right?'), height and weight were never asked at all, and there was no health-conditions question, so the clear blood work arrived because the prospect volunteered it.

P3.evidence: Deep where it counted, thin on the ladder. The future-projection question was asked properly and then pushed when the prospect hesitated — 'Whatever you feel like, like, paint me a picture' — which produced the strongest material of the call: leading by example for his son, and breaking a cultural taboo where 'even consuming protein itself is a very big taboo out there.' The rep drove that through to identity and legacy explicitly: 'you're not going to be the dad on the couch.' But the surface rungs were skipped — no one-thing-you'd-change, no mobility-versus-strength-versus-energy, no what-can't-you-do-physically — and the son, the single biggest driver on the call, was volunteered in the prospect's first answer rather than asked for, so P3f is a miss on the script's own rule. The reflect-back was a half-move: 'It's your lifestyle, not a...' / 'It's my lifestyle, exactly', rather than the scripted this-isn't-really-about-X confirmation.

P4.evidence: Ran cleanly and in order. 'You had other trainers, too?' produced the gym personal training and the HIIT block; 'I used to have these dips where I used to get fit, and then I couldn't sustain it' answered what happened; and the rep asked the why directly — 'Why do you think that happened? What was the reason?' — which surfaced both the real constraints (his son's birth, his wife's pregnancy, no home option) and the real failure mode (HIIT six to seven days a week at 45-60 minutes leaving him depleted in three weeks). The prospect named his own gap unprompted and precisely: 'What I really lack right now is actually a proper guidance and like a mentor.' The root-cause line landed later, during the spouse handling, in its natural form: 'if you could do it on your own, you won't be on the call.' Only the explicit one-thing-in-the-way question was never asked.

P5.evidence: The only genuine consequence question anywhere in this batch, asked almost verbatim: 'if nothing changes, like, where do you think, where would you be in two years, three years now?' It worked immediately and produced the emotional core of the call — 'If nothing changes, I don't know. It's quite a scary state, honestly... I just feel like I won't be there for my kid.' Then the rep stopped. He never asked whether that is something the prospect is willing to settle for, never asked why not, and never asked for a line in the sand. The prospect drew his own line unprompted, the 1 December deadline for his son's birthday, which is exactly the commitment P5d exists to manufacture and which the rep got for free without asking.

P6.evidence: The all-in question was asked in the right place, before anything was presented, and framed with the selection rationale first — 'we're making sure that people we onboard are fully committed to actually doing the work and showing up... So I have to ask you, when we make this work, are you going to show up?' The answer was unambiguous: 'Yes, I'm 100% committed to it. I feel like I've just kept it, procrastinated for a very long time. And I've decided this is the end to it.' The rep also re-confirmed after the price landed, which is the correct recovery move: 'You're still good on this. Like, you feel that this actually can get you to your goals, and you're going to be fully committed?' The belief question in its scripted form — can you get there with the right structure and the right person in your corner — was only asked in that post-price version, so P6a is partial.

P11.evidence: Payment was genuinely worked, a structure was agreed in principle and the prospect counter-proposed his own terms, but nothing was collected and no link was sent. The Trevor call was named as the destination — 'I'll walk you through the onboarding, get you on a call with Trevor in the beginning of upcoming week' — and never scheduled. The agreement, the welcome email, the Skool link and the questionnaire were not mentioned at all. What was done right, and is worth copying, is that the follow-up was pinned to a specific time on the same day with the same joining link rather than left as 'let me know': 'How about like 2.30 p.m.?' / 'Cool. So we're going to connect with the same Zoom link.' One weakness inside that: the rep could not confirm the terms the prospect asked for and had to defer — 'I'll just need to ask my supervisor' — which hands a warm buyer a two-hour gap with an unanswered question.

objection_plays.detail: The model example for this corpus. Isolated first — 'if you're saying that, okay, you're 100% in, but finances right now are the obstacle we need to take care of, all right, let's talk about it.' Asked permission before opening the books: 'do we like to explore the ways that we could potentially make this work?' Set the expectation that terms are individual: 'we don't have, like, set payment plans. It's always customized.' Then ran the financial picture in the scripted order and got answers to all of it — monthly surplus ('roughly, what's left in the tank?' / '1,000 to 1,500'), where it goes, savings ('is it like a five or four figure' / 'five figure'), other investments ('any other investments?' / some crypto), and credit cards with limits ('How many of them? And what's the limit on them?' / '60, 70k limits'). Only then did he propose structures, and both preserved the full $6,000 — half down plus three monthly thousands, or Pava financing over up to twelve months. He then let the prospect choose. The one scripted line missing is the SHOULD I versus HOW reframe. Compare with the Tom call four days earlier, where the same rep cut the price to $4,000 without ever asking any of these questions.

Ran nearly complete and produced the result. Belief and commitment were re-isolated before touching the spouse question. He asked what obstacles she might raise, got the real answer (competing household plans and the wife's new business rather than opposition), and landed the scripted reason-she-would-not-object move: 'So there would be no reason for her not wanting you getting stronger, showing up.' He then pre-framed the risk of a price-only conversation — 'the wives don't have the full picture... she asks, okay, so how much is it? And you tell the price. And then she's like, no' — and offered the three-way call. When the prospect declined and asked to speak with her privately, the rep did the strongest thing available: he sent him upstairs immediately and held the line with his camera off rather than rescheduling. Seventeen minutes later the prospect returned with 'I'm completely on board.' Missing from the play: the ownership challenge ('is this genuinely needing her input, or asking permission to bet on yourself'), which was not needed here.

The closing 'can I get maybe an hour or two? We are just crunching some numbers' was met with agreement and a pinned time, which is the right instinct — no drift, same day, same link. None of the scripted content ran, and given the prospect had already said he was completely on board, that is defensible. The soft spot is that the rep created the reason for the delay himself by not being able to authorise the instalment structure the prospect asked for.

Clinical fit. The prospect disclosed a historic low back injury from soccer plus current chronic lower back and trapezius pain, and was then taken through a programme built on kettlebell swings, which is loaded ballistic hip hinging. No question was asked about whether any clinician has assessed the back. The rep went the other way and reinforced the prospect's self-clearance by validating that a week and a half of swings had already helped. The script contains no clinical screen at all, so nothing prompted the question — but the injury check in Phase 2 stops at 'do you have any injuries' and never asks 'has anyone told you what you should not do'.

notes: Textbook money conversation — isolate, ask permission, run the full financial picture, then structure without touching the price — and it should be pulled as the training example for this team, particularly against the same rep's Tom call four days earlier where none of it ran and the price was cut instead. Two things to coach: do not promise a six-month outcome against a five-month date, and add a clearance question to the injury sequence rather than validating the prospect's own all-clear.
